title: 28 — Encryption in Practice
html:
28 — Encryption in Practice

What the algorithms are for, which layer to encrypt at, and what each layer actually protects you from — with the code, and with how banks, payment processors and chat apps really do it.

13 §3 A02 covers cryptographic failures as an OWASP category and 13 §7 covers secrets management. This file is the depth behind them. Every C# snippet was compiled and round-tripped before being written down. Sources are at the end, marked [n].

1. The decision table — start here

If you read one section, read this one.

You need to protect Encrypt at Mechanism Stops
Data crossing a network Transport TLS 1.3 Passive sniffing, tampering, MITM
A stolen disk or laptop Volume BitLocker / LUKS / dm-crypt Physical theft of powered-off media
A stolen database backup Database file TDE Backup files leaving the building
A specific sensitive column from your own DBA Application Column/field encryption, keys outside the DB Insider with DB access, memory dumps
A card number you must not hold Neither — remove it Tokenisation / a vault Breach scope; PCI audit surface
A password Nothing — you never encrypt passwords Argon2id / bcrypt hashing Credential reuse after a breach
A file at rest in blob storage Object SSE with a customer-managed key Cloud-provider-side and bucket misconfiguration
A message the server must never read End to end Signal protocol / MLS The operator, subpoenas, server compromise
Proving a payload came from you Not encryption — signing HMAC or a digital signature Forgery, replay

⚠️ The most common architectural mistake is encrypting at the wrong layer and believing you are covered. TDE on a database whose DBA can SELECT the plaintext protects you from a stolen backup tape and nothing else. That is a real control with a narrow scope — just be precise about which scope.

2. Fundamentals — three different tools

2.1 Symmetric encryption — for bulk data

One key encrypts and decrypts. Fast — gigabytes per second with hardware AES.

Algorithm Use Notes
AES-256-GCM Default choice AEAD: encrypts and authenticates. Hardware-accelerated on any modern CPU
ChaCha20-Poly1305 Mobile, no AES-NI AEAD, constant-time in software. TLS 1.3 cipher suite
AES-256-CBC + HMAC Legacy interop only Needs a separate MAC, applied encrypt-then-MAC. Easy to get wrong
AES-ECB Never Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext — the famous "ECB penguin"

AEAD is the thing to internalise. Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data gives you confidentiality and integrity in one primitive. Without it, an attacker who cannot read your ciphertext can still flip bits in it and watch what your application does — and CBC without a MAC is exploitable by padding oracle.

using System.Security.Cryptography;

public static class Aead
{
    private const int NonceSize = 12;   // 96 bits — the GCM standard
    private const int TagSize   = 16;   // 128 bits

    /// <summary>Returns nonce || ciphertext || tag as one blob.</summary>
    public static byte[] Encrypt(ReadOnlySpan<byte> key, ReadOnlySpan<byte> plaintext, ReadOnlySpan<byte> associated)
    {
        byte[] output = new byte[NonceSize + plaintext.Length + TagSize];
        Span<byte> nonce = output.AsSpan(0, NonceSize);

        // A fresh random nonce PER MESSAGE. See the warning below — this is the one that ruins you.
        RandomNumberGenerator.Fill(nonce);

        using var aes = new AesGcm(key, TagSize);
        aes.Encrypt(
            nonce,
            plaintext,
            output.AsSpan(NonceSize, plaintext.Length),
            output.AsSpan(NonceSize + plaintext.Length, TagSize),
            associated);

        return output;
    }

    public static byte[] Decrypt(ReadOnlySpan<byte> key, ReadOnlySpan<byte> blob, ReadOnlySpan<byte> associated)
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<byte> nonce = blob[..NonceSize];
        ReadOnlySpan<byte> tag = blob[^TagSize..];
        ReadOnlySpan<byte> ciphertext = blob[NonceSize..^TagSize];

        byte[] plaintext = new byte[ciphertext.Length];

        using var aes = new AesGcm(key, TagSize);
        // Throws AuthenticationTagMismatchException if the ciphertext OR the associated data was altered.
        aes.Decrypt(nonce, ciphertext, tag, plaintext, associated);

        return plaintext;
    }
}

⚠️ Never reuse a nonce with the same key in GCM. It is not a "weaker" outcome — reusing a nonce leaks the authentication subkey, letting an attacker forge arbitrary messages, and XORing the two ciphertexts reveals the XOR of the plaintexts. Either generate a random 96-bit nonce per message (safe up to ~2³² messages per key) or use a strict counter. If you cannot guarantee uniqueness, use AES-GCM-SIV, which degrades gracefully.

Associated data is the underrated parameter. It is authenticated but not encrypted, so bind the ciphertext to its context — the row id, the tenant id, the column name. Then an attacker who copies an encrypted value from row 5 into row 9 gets an authentication failure instead of a successful swap.

2.2 Asymmetric encryption — for key exchange and identity

A keypair: public key encrypts or verifies, private key decrypts or signs. Orders of magnitude slower than symmetric, so it is never used for bulk data.

Purpose Use Not
Key agreement ECDH (X25519, P-256) RSA key transport — no forward secrecy
Signatures Ed25519, ECDSA P-256 RSA-PKCS#1 v1.5 for new work
Encrypting a small blob RSA-OAEP, or better a KEM RSA-PKCS#1 v1.5 padding — Bleichenbacher

RSA-2048 versus ECC-256: roughly comparable security, but the ECC key is 32 bytes rather than 256, and operations are far faster. Prefer elliptic curve for anything new. RSA persists mainly because of certificate and hardware compatibility.

How every real protocol combines them — hybrid encryption:

  1. Asymmetric key agreement establishes a shared secret.
  2. A KDF (HKDF) derives symmetric keys from it.
  3. AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypts the actual data.

TLS does this. Signal does this. Your envelope encryption does this. Asymmetric crypto protects the key; symmetric crypto protects the data.

2.3 Hashing — not encryption at all

Hashing is one-way. There is no key and nothing to decrypt. Three distinct jobs, three distinct tools:

Job Use Why
Store a password Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, PBKDF2 Deliberately slow and memory-hard, so brute force is expensive
Fingerprint data / integrity SHA-256, SHA-3, BLAKE3 Fast is the point
Authenticate a message with a shared key HMAC-SHA256 A plain hash of secret + message is length-extendable

⚠️ "We encrypt passwords" is a red flag in any design review. Encryption is reversible, so a key compromise exposes every password. Passwords get hashed with a slow, salted, memory-hard function — and the salt is per-user, stored alongside, not secret.

// .NET 8+: PBKDF2 in the framework. Argon2id needs a library (Konscious.Security.Cryptography or libsodium).
byte[] salt = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16);
byte[] hash = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(
    password: password,
    salt: salt,
    iterations: 600_000,            // OWASP guidance moves upward over time — treat as a config value
    hashAlgorithm: HashAlgorithmName.SHA256,
    outputLength: 32);

// Comparison MUST be constant-time, or you leak the answer through timing.
bool ok = CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals(hash, storedHash);

Also note peppering: a secret value, held outside the database (in a KMS or config), mixed in alongside the salt. It means a stolen database alone is not enough to start cracking.

3. In transit — TLS

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: "ClientHello with supported suites and a key share"
    S->>C: "ServerHello, certificate, key share, Finished"
    Note over C,S: "shared secret via ECDH, keys derived with HKDF"
    C->>S: "Finished, then application data"
    Note over C,S: "TLS 1.3 completes in one round trip"
Point Why it matters
TLS 1.3 only (1.2 where legacy demands it) 1.0/1.1 are deprecated; SSLv3 is broken
Forward secrecy is mandatory in 1.3 Ephemeral ECDH means a stolen server key cannot decrypt yesterday's captures
Certificate validation is not optional Disabling validation "for now" is how MITM becomes possible in production
mTLS for service-to-service Both sides present certificates — the service identity is the certificate
HSTS Stops the downgrade-to-HTTP attack before TLS is even negotiated
Certificate pinning Only for mobile apps you ship; it makes rotation hard and can brick clients

⚠️ TLS terminating at the load balancer means the traffic behind it is plaintext. In a zero-trust or regulated environment you need TLS (usually mTLS) on the internal hops too, or a service mesh doing it for you. "We use HTTPS" describes one hop.

4. At rest — the layers, and what each one actually stops

This is the section people get wrong, so read it as a matrix rather than a list.

flowchart TB
    APP["Application-level encryption<br/>keys in a KMS, never in the DB"]
    COL["Column / field encryption<br/>Always Encrypted, pgcrypto"]
    TDE["Database file encryption — TDE<br/>data files, logs, backups"]
    VOL["Volume encryption<br/>BitLocker, LUKS"]
    DISK["Physical disk"]
    APP --> COL --> TDE --> VOL --> DISK
Threat Volume TDE Column App-level Tokenised
Someone steals the powered-off server ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔
Backup file leaks / lands in the wrong bucket ✘ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔
Attacker gets a DB login ✘ ✘ ✔ ✔ ✔
Your own DBA reads the column ✘ ✘ ✔ ✔ ✔
App server is compromised ✘ ✘ ✘ ✘* ✔
SQL injection dumping the table ✘ ✘ ✔ ✔ ✔
Memory scraped from the DB process ✘ ✘ ✔ ✔ ✔

* An app-level key held in the compromised app's memory is compromised too. Only not holding the data — tokenisation — survives a full application compromise. That is the honest limit of encryption and the reason regulators push tokenisation for card data.

4.1 TDE versus column-level, concretely

Microsoft's two mechanisms make the distinction unusually clear [3][4][5]:

TDE Always Encrypted
What it is Encrypts data files, logs and backups on disk Encrypts specific columns in the client driver
Where keys live With the database engine Only with the application — never reaches the engine
Protects against Stolen files, lost media, leaked backups DBA/insider access, memory scraping, memory dumps
Does not protect Anything with a valid DB login, including the DBA Anything the app can see
App changes None — transparent Schema and application changes required
Query cost Negligible Equality only on deterministic columns; no LIKE, ranges, or ORDER BY on randomised ones

Microsoft's own framing is worth memorising: TDE is about operational safety; Always Encrypted is about trust boundaries [3][4]. They compose — use both, plus TLS, for defence in depth [3].

4.2 What breaks when you encrypt a column

This is the practical cost, and the reason column encryption is applied surgically rather than everywhere.

Operation Randomised encryption Deterministic encryption
WHERE col = @value ✘ ✔
WHERE col LIKE 'A%' ✘ ✘
ORDER BY col, ranges ✘ ✘
JOIN ON ✘ ✔ (same key both sides)
Index usefulness None Equality only
Leaks Nothing Equal plaintexts produce equal ciphertexts — reveals distribution

⚠️ Deterministic encryption on a low-cardinality column is close to useless. Encrypt a Gender or Country column deterministically and anyone can infer the values by frequency without a key. Deterministic is for high-cardinality identifiers you must look up by — a national insurance number — not for categories.

Searching encrypted data — the blind index pattern. When you need lookup and randomised encryption, store a keyed hash beside the ciphertext:

// The searchable column: a truncated HMAC of the normalised value, under a separate key.
// Truncating deliberately creates collisions, so the index reveals a bucket rather than a value.
static byte[] BlindIndex(ReadOnlySpan<byte> indexKey, string value)
{
    string normalised = value.Trim().ToUpperInvariant();
    byte[] full = HMACSHA256.HashData(indexKey, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(normalised));
    return full[..8];                   // 64-bit bucket
}

Query by blind index to get candidate rows, then decrypt and compare exactly. You get equality search without exposing the distribution the way deterministic encryption does.

5. Application-level encryption and key management

Encryption is easy. Key management is the whole problem. A key hard-coded in appsettings.json and committed to git has bought you nothing.

5.1 Envelope encryption — the pattern to use

Do not encrypt data directly with a key from a KMS. Instead:

flowchart LR
    KMS["KMS or HSM<br/>root key never leaves"] -->|"generate + wrap"| DEK["Data encryption key<br/>random, per record or per tenant"]
    DEK -->|"AES-GCM"| DATA[Ciphertext]
    KMS -->|"wrapped DEK stored beside the data"| STORE[(Database or blob)]
    DATA --> STORE
  1. Ask the KMS for a fresh data encryption key (DEK) — you get it in plaintext and wrapped under the root key.
  2. Encrypt the data locally with the plaintext DEK, then discard it from memory.
  3. Store the wrapped DEK alongside the ciphertext.
  4. To read: send the wrapped DEK to the KMS, get the plaintext DEK back, decrypt, discard.

Why bother: bulk data never crosses the KMS (fast, cheap, no size limits), the root key never leaves the HSM, and rotating the root key means re-wrapping small DEKs rather than re-encrypting terabytes.

public sealed record Envelope(byte[] WrappedDek, byte[] Ciphertext);

public async Task<Envelope> ProtectAsync(byte[] plaintext, string recordId, CancellationToken ct)
{
    // The KMS returns both forms; only the wrapped form is ever persisted.
    (byte[] dek, byte[] wrapped) = await _kms.GenerateDataKeyAsync(ct).ConfigureAwait(false);

    try
    {
        // Bind the ciphertext to the record so a value cannot be moved between rows.
        byte[] ciphertext = Aead.Encrypt(dek, plaintext, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(recordId));
        return new Envelope(wrapped, ciphertext);
    }
    finally
    {
        // Do not wait for the GC to get round to it.
        CryptographicOperations.ZeroMemory(dek);
    }
}

5.2 The key hierarchy

Level Lives in Rotation Notes
Root / master HSM or KMS, non-exportable Years; ceremony Under split knowledge and dual control for regulated data [6]
KEK (key-encrypting key) KMS Annually Per environment or per tenant
DEK (data-encrypting key) Wrapped, next to the data Per record, or on re-encrypt Cheap to have millions of

Crypto-shredding falls out of this for free: to make one tenant's data permanently unreadable — a GDPR erasure request across backups you cannot rewrite — destroy their DEK. The ciphertext becomes noise everywhere it exists, including in tape archives. This is often the only practical way to honour deletion across immutable backups.

5.3 HSM versus KMS

Cloud KMS HSM
What Managed key service Tamper-resistant hardware, FIPS 140-3 validated
Keys exportable No No
Use when Default for most work Regulation demands it — payment HSMs for PIN and key ceremonies
Cost Per key + per operation Substantial

5.4 Doing it in EF Core

// A value converter encrypts on write and decrypts on read, transparently to the rest of the model.
public sealed class EncryptedStringConverter(IDataProtector protector)
    : ValueConverter<string, string>(
        plaintext => protector.Protect(plaintext),
        ciphertext => protector.Unprotect(ciphertext));

protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder builder)
{
    builder.Entity<Customer>()
        .Property(c => c.NationalInsuranceNumber)
        .HasConversion(new EncryptedStringConverter(_protector));
}

⚠️ A value converter silently kills server-side filtering on that column. Where(c => c.Nin == value) either fails to translate or — worse — encrypts the comparand with a fresh nonce and matches nothing. Add a blind index column for lookups and query that. This is the trap in every "just add a converter" answer.

For ASP.NET Core specifically, IDataProtector is the right default for cookies, tokens and short-lived payloads — but it is not for long-lived data at rest, because its keyring rotates and expires. Long-lived data wants envelope encryption with keys you control.

6. Tokenisation — the one that reduces scope

Encryption makes data unreadable. Tokenisation removes it entirely, replacing it with a surrogate that has no mathematical relationship to the original [7].

Encryption Tokenisation
Reversible by Anyone with the key Only the token vault
If your app is fully compromised Key is in memory — data exposed Attacker has tokens, which are worthless
Format Ciphertext, different length Can preserve format — still looks like a card number
Compliance effect Data stays in scope Removes systems from PCI scope

For card data this is the decisive argument. PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 3.3.3 requires stored PANs to be unreadable anywhere they are stored, and Requirement 3.4 accepts one-way hashing of the entire PAN, truncation (no more than first six and last four digits), tokenisation, or strong cryptography with key management [7][8]. Requirement 3.5 tightens key management with documented procedures, split knowledge and dual control [6].

The practical architecture: your application never sees a PAN. The browser posts card details straight to the processor (hosted fields or an iframe), you receive a token, and every subsequent charge, refund and reconciliation uses the token. Your database, logs and backups are then entirely outside PCI scope for stored card data — which is worth far more than any encryption you could implement.

7. File and object encryption

Layer Mechanism Protects against
Whole disk BitLocker, LUKS Theft of powered-off hardware. Nothing once booted
Filesystem EFS, fscrypt Other users on the same host
Object storage SSE-S3 / SSE-KMS / Azure SSE Provider-side storage, some misconfiguration
Client-side You encrypt before upload The provider, and a public bucket
Archive 7-Zip AES-256, age, GPG Sharing a file over an untrusted channel

⚠️ Server-side encryption does not protect against a misconfigured public bucket. The service decrypts transparently for anyone authorised to read the object — and "public" means authorised. SSE protects against someone walking out with the physical drives. If the threat is your own access control, you need client-side encryption, where the provider never has the key.

For large files, encrypt in chunks with a per-chunk nonce derived from a counter, so you can seek and resume rather than needing the whole file in memory.

8. End-to-end encryption — chat

E2E means the operator cannot read the content, even under legal compulsion, even with full server access. That is a much stronger claim than "encrypted in transit and at rest", and it forces real design constraints.

The Signal protocol — used by Signal and WhatsApp [9][12] — has two parts [9]:

  1. X3DH handshake. Combines long-term identity keys, a signed pre-key and one-time pre-keys, so Alice can establish a session with Bob while Bob is offline — the asynchrony that makes it work for messaging [10].
  2. Double Ratchet. Every message derives a new symmetric key from the previous state, giving forward secrecy (a key compromised today cannot decrypt yesterday) and post-compromise security (the session heals once the attacker loses access) [9][11].
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Alice
    participant S as Server
    participant B as Bob (offline)
    B->>S: "publish identity key, signed pre-key, one-time pre-keys"
    A->>S: fetch Bob's pre-key bundle
    Note over A: "X3DH derives a shared secret locally"
    A->>S: "encrypted message plus Alice's ephemeral public key"
    Note over S: "the server stores ciphertext it cannot read"
    B->>S: come online and fetch
    Note over B: "derive the same secret, then ratchet forward"

What E2E costs you, and what to say when asked:

Capability Why it becomes hard
Server-side search The server has only ciphertext — search must happen on-device
Multi-device Each device is a separate identity; you need per-device sessions and key syncing
Backup An encrypted backup needs a key the user must not lose — hence recovery codes or HSM-backed key vaults
Spam and abuse detection No content to inspect; must rely on metadata and reporting
Compliance archiving Fundamentally at odds with E2E — this is the real reason many enterprise chat tools are not E2E

⚠️ Metadata is not protected by E2E. Who talked to whom, when, how often, and how much — all still visible to the operator. Sealed-sender and similar techniques narrow this, but "E2E encrypted" never means "no observable metadata".

8.1 The post-quantum ratchet

Signal has extended this against future quantum attack. PQXDH hybridises the classical X25519 agreement with a post-quantum KEM (Kyber/ML-KEM), so an attacker must break both — breaking only the elliptic curve part is insufficient [9][11]. The newer Triple Ratchet runs a sparse post-quantum ratchet alongside the Double Ratchet, using both only to produce message keys [11].

The motivating threat is harvest-now-decrypt-later: an adversary records ciphertext today and decrypts it once a quantum computer exists. For a chat message that may not matter in ten years; for a medical record, a state secret, or a 30-year mortgage, it does.

9. How banks and payment systems actually do it

Layers, not a single control:

flowchart TB
    POS["Card terminal<br/>P2PE: encrypts at the read head"] -->|"encrypted, keys the merchant never holds"| PROC[Processor]
    BROWSER["Browser hosted fields"] -->|"PAN goes straight to the processor"| PROC
    PROC --> VAULT[(Token vault)]
    PROC --> HSM["Payment HSM<br/>PIN blocks, key ceremonies"]
    MERCH["Merchant application"] -->|"token only"| PROC
    MERCH --> DB[(Database: tokens, no PANs)]
    PROC --> NET["Card network"] --> ISSUER[Issuer]
Control What it does
P2PE The terminal encrypts card data at the point of read; the merchant's systems never see plaintext
Tokenisation Merchant stores tokens, so the database is out of PCI scope for stored PANs [7][8]
Payment HSM PIN translation and key operations inside tamper-resistant hardware, never in software
Key ceremony Root keys assembled from components held by different officers — split knowledge, dual control [6]
EMV chip Per-transaction cryptogram, so a captured transaction cannot be replayed
3-D Secure Moves authentication to the issuer, shifting liability
HMAC on messages Every message between parties is authenticated, not just encrypted
Daily reconciliation Assume drift and detect it, rather than trusting the crypto to be sufficient

The single most valuable idea here for ordinary applications: the strongest way to protect sensitive data is to not be holding it. Every other control is mitigation for data you chose to keep.

10. Post-quantum — where this is actually going

NIST finalised its first post-quantum standards in August 2024 after an eight-year process: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key encapsulation and ML-DSA (FIPS 204) for signatures [1][2].

Deployment is hybrid, not replacement: TLS combines classical X25519 with ML-KEM-768 as X25519MLKEM768, so the connection is safe if either holds [1][2]. Adoption is already substantial — Cloudflare has hybrid ML-KEM enabled by default at its edge with more than half of human traffic using post-quantum key agreement, AWS rolled it out to KMS and then to ACM and Secrets Manager, and around 49% of measured domains show at least partial post-quantum readiness in 2026 [1][2].

Primitive Quantum-vulnerable? Migration
AES-256 Largely fine — Grover halves the effective bits Nothing urgent
SHA-256/384 Fine for collision resistance Nothing urgent
RSA, ECDH, ECDSA Broken by Shor's algorithm ML-KEM for agreement, ML-DSA for signatures

⚠️ What to do now is not "rewrite your crypto". It is crypto-agility: know where every algorithm is used, avoid hard-coding them, keep certificate and key rotation working, and prefer TLS libraries that already negotiate hybrid suites. The barrier to migration is reported as operational rather than cryptographic — legacy appliances and validation, not missing standards [1].

11. Mistakes that keep recurring

Mistake Why it is bad
Rolling your own crypto or mode Every subtle detail is exploitable; use vetted primitives
ECB mode Leaks plaintext structure
Nonce or IV reuse with GCM Catastrophic — key recovery and forgery
Encrypting passwords Reversible; hash with Argon2id/bcrypt instead
A key in source control or appsettings.json The key is now as widely distributed as the repository
MD5/SHA-1 for anything security-relevant Collisions are practical
Non-constant-time comparison of MACs or hashes Timing side channel
CBC without a MAC Padding oracle
"We use HTTPS, so we're encrypted" One hop, in transit only
TDE presented as protection from insiders It is not — any valid login reads plaintext
Deterministic encryption on low-cardinality data Frequency analysis recovers values without a key
No rotation plan A key you cannot rotate is a key you cannot recover from
Logging the plaintext you just encrypted The most common way encrypted data leaks

12. Checklist

  • TLS 1.3 everywhere, including internal hops; certificate validation never disabled
  • AEAD (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) for all symmetric encryption, with a unique nonce per message
  • Associated data binds each ciphertext to its record and context
  • Passwords hashed with Argon2id/bcrypt/PBKDF2 at current cost parameters, compared in constant time
  • Keys in a KMS or HSM, never in configuration or source; envelope encryption for data at rest
  • A documented, rehearsed key rotation procedure — including the compromise path
  • Card data tokenised, not encrypted, and out of scope wherever possible
  • Correct layer chosen per threat, and the gaps written down rather than assumed covered
  • Crypto-shredding available for erasure requests that reach immutable backups
  • An inventory of algorithms in use, so post-quantum migration is a change and not an excavation

Interview angle. "How would you protect this sensitive field?" has a weak answer and a strong one. Weak: "encrypt it with AES." Strong: "First — do we need to store it at all? If not, tokenise. If we do, what is the threat? A stolen backup is TDE. An untrusted DBA is application-level encryption with keys in a KMS the database cannot reach, envelope-encrypted, with a blind index if we need to search it. And I'd want the rotation and erasure story before writing any of it."
